candidate.answerReason: Milk permits only 7/4 of the original recipe, less than the amounts permitted by chocolate or sugar. This produces 5 × 7/4 = 8 3/4 servings.

methods.label: Compare how many batches each supply allows
methods.explanation:
Call the original recipe one batch. Keeping the ingredient ratios fixed means that every ingredient amount and the number of servings must be multiplied by the same factor.

Compare how many batches each supply can support:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Chocolate: }&5\div2=\frac{5}{2},\\
\text{Sugar: }&2\div\frac14=8,\\
\text{Milk: }&7\div4=\frac74.
\end{aligned}
\]
Water imposes no restriction. The smallest of these amounts is \(\frac74\), so Jordan can make that many batches without exceeding any supply. Any larger amount would require more than her \(7\) cups of milk.

Each batch makes \(5\) servings, giving
\[
5\cdot\frac74=\frac{35}{4}=8\frac34
\]
servings. The answer is \(\boxed{8\frac34}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: Comparing recipe multipliers uses elementary ratios and fractions, with no formal inequality system needed.

candidate.annotationRationale: Direct proportion governs the common scaling of ingredients and servings. Ratio meaning, fraction division, and multiplication by an integer support the batch-capacity calculations. The smallest capacity proves both feasibility and maximality.

review.mathematicalCheck: The supplies allow \(5/2\), 8, and \(7/4\) batches respectively. Their minimum, \(7/4\), is feasible and any larger amount exceeds the milk supply. It yields \(35/4=8\frac34\) servings.
